claims.text: The Cr-free Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr alloy is a single-phase BCC alloy.
Asymmetric XRD peaks in the Cr-free alloy arise from dendritic versus interdendritic micro-segregation.
The Cr-free alloy has low room-temperature fracture strain because of micro-segregation.
The Cr-free baseline contains no Laves phase.
Adding approximately 4 at.% Cr induces a C14 Laves phase in Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr.
The Cr-induced C14 Laves phase occupies approximately 4 vol.%.
The C14 Laves phase forms a reticulated, interconnected network.
Cr remains as a solute in the BCC matrix and contracts its lattice parameter.
Cr-associated lattice distortion produces solid-solution hardening.
Cr supplies a thermodynamic driving force for formation of a Cr-rich Laves phase.
The reticulated Laves phase can impede crack extension through crack bridging and deflection.
The interconnected C14 Laves phase creates a percolating brittle path that promotes crack initiation and rapid propagation.
The brittle Laves-phase network keeps fracture strain low or decreases it despite hardening.
Cr addition increases yield strength through solid-solution hardening.
The Cr-modified alloy will exhibit a distinct XRD signature from a C14 Laves phase.
Approximately 4 at.% Cr is sufficient to cross the solubility limit for Laves-phase formation but insufficient to produce a fully Laves-phase microstructure.
Homogenization below the matrix melting point and cooling that does not suppress precipitation will permit Laves-phase nucleation.

Comparing identically processed Cr-free and 4 at.% Cr alloys by synchrotron XRD, microscopy, and in-situ tensile testing can distinguish Cr-specific phase formation from baseline micro-segregation effects.

contradictions.description: The Cr-modified material contains six elements, but the uncertainty field calls it a 'specific quinary system.'
